**This is a pre-release for testing.** It is not marked Latest and is not intended for general use. If you want a stable build, use v0.4.6.

Linux x86_64 only — this pre-release ships the tarball. No `.deb`, `.rpm` or AUR package is built for previews.

alpha.3 was billed as the last alpha. It isn't: the long-haul flight it asked for produced a finding worth shipping before the line moves to beta.

---

## The headline: the thread pool no longer inflates the heap

alpha.3 asked for a six-hour-plus flight. That flight ran 12 hours, and the trace showed the process holding **6,166 MB of heap while only 572 MB of it was in use.** Live data was flat across a *18× increase* in work — nothing was leaking — yet the heap kept climbing in discrete ~420 MB steps.

Every one of those steps landed on a sample where the thread count was at its ceiling: **581 threads.**

That number is tokio's doing. Its blocking thread pool defaults to 512 threads, and ours carries DDS encoding and disk I/O, so under sustained prefetch it saturates. glibc hands each thread a heap arena to avoid lock contention, each arena keeps its own high-water mark, and that space is never returned. Every excursion to 581 threads recruited fresh arenas and ratcheted the total.

The pool is now sized from what the work actually needs — the CPU and disk I/O pool capacities plus a reserve — rather than from tokio's default. On a 32-core machine that is 136 blocking threads instead of 512.

### Measured

FAOR→EGLL, 11 hours, 121,641 textures generated, against the alpha.3 baseline flight at **matched work** rather than matched time:

| textures generated | alpha.3 | alpha.4 | |
|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 5,000 | 6,473 MB | 5,026 MB | 22% less |
| 40,000 | 8,640 MB | 7,258 MB | 16% less |
| 55,000 | 9,812 MB | 7,209 MB | 27% less |
| 90,000 | 11,936 MB | 9,441 MB | **21% less** |

Peak thread count fell from 581 to 205. Throughput was unaffected — around 3.1 textures per second sustained across the flight.

### What we are *not* claiming

**This does not close #227 either.** The run ended at 11,580 MB against alpha.3's 11,876 — the same ceiling, reached after 35% more work. The growth is slower, not stopped; heap ratcheting still runs at roughly 44 MB per thousand textures.

Two of three contributors are now dealt with. The third — glibc accumulating arena high-water marks — is understood and has a candidate fix, but it is not in this build.

**If you want to help with that one**, you can test it without a rebuild:

```bash
MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=4 xearthlayer run
```

If memory holds noticeably flatter with that set, please say so on #227. Watch for any drop in scene-load speed, which is the thing that variable can cost.

---

## Removed: `cache.disk_io_profile`

This setting never did anything. It was read, validated, and passed to a concurrency limiter that nothing ever consulted — three separate code paths computed a value from it and none of them reached a live limiter.

It has been removed, along with the setup-wizard question that asked you to choose one.

**Nothing to do.** An existing config with the setting still loads; the line is simply ignored. To tidy it up:

```bash
xearthlayer config upgrade
```

That removes it and reports what it removed. A backup is written first. Storage-type detection is unaffected — `xearthlayer setup` still reports whether your cache lives on NVMe, SSD or a spinning disk.

---

## What to fly

Long. The value of this build is entirely in the tail — the first two hours of any flight now look fine on every version we have shipped. **Six hours or more, and longer is better.**

If you hit an out-of-memory kill, the log is the useful artifact:

```
~/.xearthlayer/xearthlayer.log
```

It is overwritten on every launch, so copy it aside before relaunching. Attach it to #227 along with your core count and configured cache sizes.

One known gap worth mentioning: memory is sampled once a minute, so a short spike between samples leaves no trace. If you see the system momentarily balloon and recover, that is real and we cannot see it — please report what you observed and roughly how long it lasted.
